planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into rocky, well-drained soil in partial shade; check local white pine blister rust planting restrictions before adding Ribes in states that regulate the genus.

directions: Native to rocky uplands, bluffs, and riparian woodlands across Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Arkansas, Tennessee, Georgia, and Alabama, this is the most genuinely southern Ribes available, tolerating the warmer end of the genus's range better than the northern gooseberries already in the collection. Clove-scented reddish flowers in short clusters precede small, black, acid-flavored berries best used cooked into jam or jelly rather than eaten fresh. It is sold by at least one specialty native nursery, giving it real commercial availability unlike some rarer regional Ribes.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this is a dry-heat and drought-tolerant Great Basin species, not a humid-climate selection.

directions: Native to semiarid sagebrush, woodland, and pine habitats across Montana, Idaho, Washington, Oregon, Utah, Nevada, California, and Arizona, adapted to hot, dry summers and cold, snowy winters with very little annual precipitation. This is a xeriscape candidate for arid-climate gardens rather than the humid Southeast, since its heat tolerance is paired with a strict need for dry air and fast-draining soil. Spreading, arching, multi-branched habit with small white to yellowish spring flowers.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into rocky, fast-draining slope soil in full to partial sun, mimicking Mediterranean-climate chaparral and oak woodland.

directions: A California, Baja California, and Arizona chaparral and oak-woodland native growing on rocky, fast-draining slopes from sea level to high elevation. Arching, densely spiny stems carry reflexed yellow sepals and edible black berries. Genuinely drought and dry-heat tolerant under a Mediterranean-summer rainfall pattern, making it a good fit for California, Arizona, or Texas Hill Country xeriscaping rather than humid Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into rocky, well-drained alpine-style soil in a cool, high-elevation site; will not perform in warm, humid, or low-elevation gardens.

directions: A true alpine and subalpine dwarf shrub ranging from British Columbia to California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Wyoming, found on exposed ridges, open talus, and rocky slopes at high elevation. Bright red, glandular-bristly berries ripen on a low, spiny mound, best suited to an alpine rock garden or high-elevation native planting rather than a warm lowland site. It is the opposite of heat-tolerant and should be reserved for cold-climate or high-elevation gardens.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into rocky, well-drained canyon soil in full to partial sun, mimicking high-elevation conifer canyon habitat.

directions: Native to high-elevation coniferous canyons of the southern Rockies and Southwest, including Colorado, New Mexico, the Texas Trans-Pecos, Arizona, and Utah, typically found at 5,600 to 10,000 feet. Though Texas is technically a Gulf state, this is a cool, dry, high-elevation species with no lowland Gulf Coast relevance. Small, spiny stems carry slender tubular flowers distinct from the broader-petaled currants already in the collection.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into moist, humus-rich montane forest soil in partial shade, mimicking Klamath-Siskiyou conifer understory.

directions: Endemic to the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains of southwest Oregon and northwest California, growing in montane and subalpine conifer forest understory. Dark red, prickly, edible-but-astringent berries ripen in early fall, best cooked rather than eaten fresh. A regional endemic with no heat or southern relevance, included purely to broaden native Ribes species diversity in the collection.
